changes.before:
Culture is what people learn from what actually happens around them. Staff watch which work is praised at all-staff meetings, which requests get budget and which shortcuts nobody questions. Those patterns teach more than any values statement. In a division, they are set less by what the senior leader says than by what the senior leader recognizes, resources and tolerates, often without noticing.

A useful first step is to compare the stated values with three plain lists. What did we recognize last year, in awards, praise and announcements? What did we resource, in staff time, budget and leadership attention? What did we tolerate, such as late answers to partners, meetings where the same people always speak, or rushed decisions that skipped the people affected? Put each list beside the values the division publishes and ask where they match and where they do not. Keep each list short and concrete; three or four items is enough to start an honest conversation with your managers.

Deloitte's research on inclusive leadership treats fairness as more than identical treatment. It looks at fair outcomes, fair processes and clear communication about decisions, and it names promotions, rewards and work assignments as places where personal and process bias show up. At division scale, ask who is affected by what you reward. Whose work is missing from what you celebrate, perhaps because it is slow, relational or done with partners? How would you find out without relying only on the people already closest to leadership?

Start with your own defaults. Many leaders learned to reward speed, visible output and confidence in meetings because those were rewarded for them. They can be good things, and they can also hide careful work, partnership with people who receive services, and contributions from staff who work differently. The Center for Creative Leadership's REAL framework begins with Reveal: discovering how your own organization works, including norms that often go unnoticed, before choosing what to change. Its other elements, Elevate equity, Activate diversity and Lead inclusively, work alongside Reveal as complementary lenses, not stages to pass through. Look at patterns across the division, never at individuals. Promotion, pay and selection decisions stay with Human Resources and its processes; your part is the signals around them.

changes.before:
Senior leaders send signals whether or not they mean to. What you ask about in meetings tells managers what matters. What you fund, delay or cut tells them what is real. Who briefs executives or leads cross-division work tells staff what kind of person gets ahead here, and who is heard before a decision tells them whose knowledge counts. Small choices add up, because a whole division is watching them.

Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide describes how leaders send signals across a whole organization. At its in-progress stage, a leader shares successes with a key group only and relies on limited data sources without seeking diverse opinions. A proficient leader builds trust through follow-through and transparent communication, and draws on feedback from collaborators and community leaders. Each of these can be checked against your own calendar and decisions.

The intercultural continuum can describe an organization's practices, not only personal growth. IDI, LLC describes its orientations, and Milton Bennett's developmental model adds Integration. A Minimization practice sounds fair: anyone may speak at the briefing, and the same fast question-and-answer format is used for all. An Acceptance practice notices that the format favors people who think aloud quickly, already know the executives and need no interpreter or reading time. An Adaptation practice changes the routine, with materials sent early, written questions accepted, interpreters booked by default and authors briefing their own work. An Integration practice makes moving between ways of contributing an ordinary part of planning and deciding.

To read your own signals, look at a month of your calendar, your last few budget decisions and who has briefed executives or led cross-division work, by unit and role, not person by person. Ask what you are treating as normal and where you learned it. The National Equity Project contrasts pyramid leadership, top-down and built around delivering a message, which it calls the dominant culture default, with circle leadership, which listens, shares leadership and seeks input from those most affected and furthest from power. Selection and promotion follow Human Resources processes; your part is who gets the experience and visibility those processes later count. Then ask a few people who rarely brief executives what it would take for them to do so, choose one format to change, and tell people why.

Examples from the Intercultural Development Continuum can help examine a meeting format. A Minimization example offers everyone the same fast question-and-answer session without asking what access or preparation it requires. An Acceptance example recognizes that people have different needs and ways of contributing. An Adaptation example changes the format: materials arrive early, written questions are welcomed and needed communication support is arranged with participants. These are illustrations, not assessments of a person, team or organization. Offering several formats also does not establish that every participant can use them; check what is needed and whether the changes work.

To read your own signals, review a month of meetings and recent decisions about budgets or presentations. Look at which roles and units have opportunities, and ask what assumptions shaped those choices. The National Equity Project contrasts a directive approach for problems with known solutions with shared inquiry for complex problems whose solutions must be developed. Its framework does not make every directive decision wrong or remove formal accountability. Ask willing staff what helps or prevents them from contributing, and examine criteria, workload and access with responsible managers. Visibility is not a promise of promotion. Change an authorized meeting format, explain why and review who can participate.

changes.before:
A division cannot learn what working there is like only from whoever speaks up most. Engagement surveys, stay conversations and the concerns people raise each show part of the picture. Each also carries a risk that someone feels exposed. Listening at scale means gathering enough to see patterns while keeping every individual safe. It also means people can see what happened as a result.

Minnesota Management and Budget's FAQ for the 2025 enterprise engagement and inclusion survey sets out its protections. Only the unit that runs the survey knows who answered. Information that could identify a respondent is private under state data practices law. Groups with fewer than 10 respondents are combined with larger ones. Results are not used to evaluate individual managers or employees, and the survey is not a way to report misconduct; that goes to Human Resources or as agency policy provides. MMB recommends that leaders share results with employees and build action plans with them.

Carry the survey's privacy protections into how you lead. Read results by question and group, and never try to work out who wrote a comment; a distinctive comment can identify someone even without a name. If a theme points at one team, look at its routines, not at who said what. Stay conversations, in which supervisors ask what keeps people and what might lead them to leave, can add depth when supervisors bring back themes, not names, and nobody keeps notes about named individuals. Washington State's enterprise leadership competencies ask leaders to remove fear from organizational culture, and how you handle what you hear is where staff decide whether that is true.

Return what you heard, and say what you will do about it. Within a set time, tell people what you learned, what you will do, what you will not do and why, and when you will report again. Ask who was not heard, such as night shifts, remote staff, people using another language or access method, or units with few respondents. If a comment describes discrimination, harassment or a safety risk, route it to Human Resources or the equal opportunity office. A report back that admits limits builds more trust than a promise that cannot be kept.
changes.after:
A division learns about work through surveys, stay conversations and concerns people raise directly. Each source shows part of the picture, and none guarantees that everyone has been heard. Plan how information will be collected, used, stored and shared before inviting people to contribute. Explain the limits of confidentiality and how required reports will be handled. A useful listening process reduces unnecessary exposure and shows what changed because people contributed.

Minnesota Management and Budget’s FAQ describes the 2025 enterprise engagement and inclusion survey. Management Analysis and Development, or MAD, administered it and knew who responded. Identifying information was protected under state law, with disclosure only as allowed by law. MAD removed identifying information from agency data and combined groups with fewer than 10 respondents. The FAQ says results are not for individual performance evaluations, and the survey is not a misconduct-reporting channel. It recommends sharing results and developing action plans with staff. These are the stated arrangements for that survey; check current guidance before describing another survey’s protections.

Work from the authorized reports and data, and do not try to identify comment authors. A distinctive phrase or small group can reveal someone even after names are removed. Ask responsible survey and data-practices staff what can be shared, then describe themes without unnecessary identifying detail. A low score may prompt inquiry, but it does not establish a particular cause or prove misconduct. Individual concerns still deserve an appropriate response even when no wider pattern is known.

Stay conversations ask what helps a person remain in a role and what might lead them to leave. They do not inherit the enterprise survey’s protections. Tell staff what notes are needed, who may receive them and what confidentiality cannot be promised. Share suitable themes in general discussion while retaining necessary records under applicable rules. Do not omit a required report, destroy records or promise that no information about individuals will be kept. A facilitator outside the reporting line may help participation, but a group session cannot guarantee anonymity.

Report back on what you learned, what you can change, what you cannot change and when you will update staff. Consider whose experience is missing and offer accessible ways to contribute without pressure to disclose personal details. Follow the reporting duties for your role. HR/LR Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations immediately to the designated office. Follow DHS referral and consultation procedures rather than investigating through a listening session. Address urgent danger through the applicable emergency or safety route; do not wait for a survey cycle or an action-plan meeting.
changes.reason: Clarify privacy and survey limits, records and reporting duties, access, leadership authority and evidence.

changes.before:
Culture changes through routines, not announcements. A values campaign, a slogan or a long list of initiatives rarely outlasts the leader who launched it. A changed routine, such as how work is assigned, how a meeting runs or how a partner's question gets answered, changes what people do every week. Over time, what people do becomes what the division is. Leaders often reach for visible launches because they show commitment quickly; the harder work is changing the ordinary steps people repeat.

The United States Office of Personnel Management built a federal inclusion measure on the idea that repeated behaviors form inclusive habits. Its 2017 report, now historical, said individual behaviors repeated over time create an inclusive work environment, and grouped those habits as fair, open, cooperative, supportive and empowering. The point still holds. Pick one structure where the gap between stated values and practice is clear and widely felt, and change that first. Choose one whose change people would notice within weeks.

Involve the people the routine affects before you redesign it. Ask frontline staff, partners and, where it fits, people who receive services how it works for them now and what would make it better. Decide together what you will look at, for whom and when. Their knowledge of where the routine breaks is often the best evidence you have, and involving them is itself a signal about whose experience counts. The National Equity Project calls this leading from the inside out, in three moves it names See, Engage and Act: understand yourself and the system, make sense of the situation with others, then try small tests with the people affected instead of one large fix. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide describes expert organizational leaders as explaining the change, monitoring results and adjusting plans. Its expert description for leading others adds disrupting norms and patterns that keep inequities in place.

Stay with a change long enough to see what it did. Most changes feel awkward for months and fade when leaders move to the next priority. Review at the times you set: what happened, for whom, and what will you keep, change or stop? Write the new routine into procedures and handover notes so it belongs to the function, not to one champion. Tell staff and partners what you learned at each review, including what did not work. Where a change touches duties, schedules or anything a labor agreement covers, bring in Human Resources and labor relations early.
changes.after:
Culture change needs follow-through in daily work. A values campaign can explain a direction, but it does not by itself change how people experience the work. A changed routine, such as how work is assigned, how a meeting runs or how a partner's question gets answered, changes what people do every week. Over time, what people do becomes what the division is. Leaders often reach for visible launches because they show commitment quickly; the harder work is changing the ordinary steps people repeat.

The United States Office of Personnel Management built a federal inclusion measure on the idea that repeated behaviors form inclusive habits. Its 2017 report, now historical, said individual behaviors repeated over time create an inclusive work environment, and grouped those habits as fair, open, cooperative, supportive and empowering. This is a useful way to examine practice, not proof that one change will transform a division. Choose a routine where evidence suggests a gap, and propose a feasible improvement within your authority. Set a realistic review period based on the work and the people affected.

Involve the people the routine affects before you redesign it. Ask frontline staff, partners and, where it fits, people who receive services how it works for them now and what would make it better. Decide together what you will look at, for whom and when. Their experience can reveal problems that other evidence misses. Consider it alongside service data and required standards, and explain how their input affects the proposal. The National Equity Project calls this leading from the inside out, in three moves it names See, Engage and Act: understand yourself and the system, make sense of the situation with others, then try small tests with the people affected instead of one large fix. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide describes expert organizational leaders as explaining the change, monitoring results and adjusting plans. Its expert description for leading others adds disrupting norms and patterns that keep inequities in place.

Give a change enough time and support to learn from it, while monitoring for harm. Set access safeguards, stop conditions and a responsible reviewer before a trial. Do not treat harm as ordinary adjustment or wait for the planned review when action is needed. Review at the times you set: what happened, for whom, and what will you keep, change or stop? Once a change is authorized, update the appropriate procedures and handover records so others can maintain and reassess it. Tell staff and partners what you learned at each review, including what did not work. Before changing duties, schedules or matters covered by a labor agreement, involve Human Resources and labor relations. A small test does not waive these requirements or required agency equity analysis.
changes.reason: Clarify privacy and survey limits, records and reporting duties, access, leadership authority and evidence.

before.title: Bennett, M. J., Towards Ethnorelativism: A Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity, IDR Institute
before.note: Supports lesson 2's use of Integration, the far point of the continuum, drawn from Bennett's developmental model. Applied here to routines and systems, never to people.

before.title: Center for Creative Leadership, The Research Foundations for REAL: A Framework for Leadership Action in Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (2023)
before.note: Supports lesson 1's description of REAL: Reveal as discovering an organization's often unnoticed norms, and the four elements as complementary lenses, not stages. Copyrighted and trademarked; ideas paraphrased. A practitioner framework that reports no validation study of its own.

before.title: National Equity Project, Leading for Equity Framework (2024)
before.note: Supports lesson 2's contrast of pyramid and circle leadership, the circle leadership card, and lesson 4's inside-out stance of See, Engage and Act with small tests. Copyrighted; ideas paraphrased. A practitioner model written for schools, not outcome research.

after.title: Minnesota Management and Budget, Enterprise Leader Competency Definition Guide (March 2024)
after.note: Supports lesson 2's Leading the Organization stages (sharing successes with a key group only, limited data sources, follow-through) and lesson 4's change rationale and monitoring, plus the Leading Others item on disrupting inequitable norms.

after.title: Minnesota Management and Budget, 2025 Enterprise Employee Engagement and Inclusion Survey: Frequently Asked Questions
after.note: Supports lesson 3 on survey privacy, combining groups under 10, no use for individual evaluations, misconduct going to Human Resources, and sharing results with staff. Describes the 2025 survey only.

after.title: Deloitte University Press, The six signature traits of inclusive leadership (2016)
after.note: Supports lesson 1 on fairness in outcomes, processes and communication, and on promotions, rewards and assignments as places bias appears. 2016 consulting research based on interviews with leaders in six countries, mostly outside government.

after.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management, 2017 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey Governmentwide Management Report
after.note: Supports lesson 4's statement that repeated behaviors form inclusive habits, and the five habits named. A historical federal measure from 2017; pages on the inclusion measure only were read.

after.title: IDI, LLC, The Intercultural Development Inventory
after.note: Defines the continuum orientations. Meeting examples illustrate concepts and do not assess individuals, teams or organizations.

after.title: Center for Creative Leadership, The Research Foundations for REAL: A Framework for Leadership Action in Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (2023)
after.note: Supports examining organizational norms and using REAL’s four elements as complementary lenses, not stages. A research-informed practitioner framework; the course does not claim that applying it proves local outcomes.

after.title: National Equity Project, Leading for Equity Framework (2024)
after.note: Supports lesson 2's contrast of pyramid and circle leadership, the circle leadership card, and lesson 4's inside-out stance of See, Engage and Act with small tests. Copyrighted; ideas paraphrased. A practitioner model written for schools, not outcome research.

after.title: DHS — Equity Policy
after.note: Required agency equity analysis and learning are not waived by an optional improvement exercise.

after.title: Minnesota Statutes 13.05 — Duties of responsible authority
after.note: Data collection, use and disclosure duties apply to mapping and analysis; removing names does not automatically make information public.

after.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited (revised 2024)
after.note: Supports supervisors’ immediate reporting duties for protected-class harassment or discrimination and the prohibition on retaliation.

after.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation Policy
after.note: Supports employee reporting expectations, supervisors' prompt referral and consultation responsibilities, and the role of Equal Opportunity and Access in assessing and investigating complaints. The public copy uses an earlier organizational name; confirm current procedures and contacts on the DHS intranet.

after.title: Minnesota Statutes 13.64 — Management and Budget data
after.note: Data classifications underlying the 2025 survey FAQ are specific to the statutory conditions; they do not automatically apply to local listening sessions.

changes.reason: Clarify privacy and survey limits, records and reporting duties, access, leadership authority and evidence.

sourceChecks.evidence: Primary 20-page guide, organizational leadership and leading others sections distinguish behavior examples and expectations; not a validated prediction that one routine will transform culture.

sourceChecks.source: MMB 2025 survey FAQ and Minnesota Statutes 13.64
sourceChecks.evidence: Primary five-page FAQ: MAD knows respondents, removes identifying details, combines groups under ten, prohibits individual performance-evaluation use and directs misconduct to agency procedures. Privacy is subject to law and specific to that survey.
Primary 32-page report pages 15–16 describes outcome, process and communication fairness; consulting research is not proof about a DHS unit.
Primary 24-page paper describes the four elements as complementary lenses rather than predetermined stages.
Primary six-page framework distinguishes directive approaches for known problems from shared inquiry for complex problems; does not make all directive decisions wrong.

sourceChecks.source: OPM 2017 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey report
sourceChecks.evidence: Primary 36-page report, page 13 describes the historical New IQ measure and five inclusion habits; retained as a historical model, not proof that a particular intervention works.
Primary resource page describes assessed orientations. Meeting examples do not classify a person, group or organization.

sourceChecks.source: MMB 1436, DHS discrimination policy, DHS Equity Policy and Minnesota Statutes 13.05
sourceChecks.evidence: Primary guidance confirms supervisors’ immediate reporting/referral duties, required equity analysis and authorized data handling. Listening sessions do not replace these duties.

sourceChecks.source: Washington leadership comparison and Bennett Integration analogy
sourceChecks.evidence: Removed the unnecessary comparison and the organizational Integration analogy. IDR chapter page returned 503; the remaining lesson uses the verified IDI concepts without conflating models.

remainingReview: Read final generated overview and job aid; complete separate whole-course acceptance.
assessmentNote: All knowledge-check answer strings, scenario choices and recommended indices preserved. Knowledge-check questions 2 and 3 clarify illustration and 2025 survey context; questions 1 and 4 remain unchanged.
